Configure your server

Self-host sandbox / computer providers

SANDBOX_PROVIDER selects where bot computers run. Workspace bots share a Team Computer by default; Private Computers are optional. See computer runtime and isolation for the sharing and persistence contract.

Quick pick

Goal Set Also need
Local Docker computers SANDBOX_PROVIDER=docker SANDBOX_SUPERVISOR_TOKEN, computer image, Docker socket for supervisor
UI only, no computers SANDBOX_PROVIDER=none No provider credential; published-images Compose still requires SANDBOX_SUPERVISOR_TOKEN
Managed remote desktop e2b / novita / daytona / createos / boat / boxd / instabox SANDBOX_SUPERVISOR_TOKEN (published-images Compose), matching API key (and optional URL knobs for Daytona/CreateOS/Boat)
One pod per computer on your own cluster SANDBOX_PROVIDER=kubernetes API and worker running in the cluster, a namespace and a Role that can create, read, delete and exec into pods
One app container per computer on your own Incus server SANDBOX_PROVIDER=incus Incus API address, a client certificate restricted to one project, and a route from the API, worker and web to the computers’ network

Published-images Compose defaults to docker. It always starts the supervisor and requires SANDBOX_SUPERVISOR_TOKEN, including for none and remote providers. This stack credential does not replace a remote provider’s API key.

Settings configuration

Set COMPUTER_SETTINGS_ENABLED=true on the API to turn this on. Admins can then choose Settings → Computer → New computers run on and save a supported provider’s fields. The API supplies the provider’s field descriptors and validates values server-side. Credentials are encrypted in the secret store and never returned; a blank secret field keeps its saved value for the same provider and destination. Changing a URL requires credentials again. Default uses SANDBOX_PROVIDER. Docker, Kubernetes, Incus, desktop, fake, and none remain environment-only. Settings overrides are disabled for desktop and fake deployments.

The account form offers only providers that declare support for account-owned computers. Team Computers follow their owner’s account choice; Private Computers use the deployment choice. See Wuying setup for that adapter’s fields and requirements.

Choosing a provider

The Electron desktop app is a client of the same API. Docker remains the default. For an app-managed local instance, the local operator can choose Use this Mac (macOS) or Use this computer (Windows/Linux). After native confirmation, an authenticated bridge sends commands from the Docker backend to Electron, where they run under your OS account. Computer Access… in the app menu changes the choice; Revoke Local Computer Access immediately disconnects active operations and revokes the saved permission. Local execution requires the desktop app to remain running. Connecting to an existing remote instance does not grant it access to your computer. Browser and mobile clients use the deployment’s configured computer; they do not expose their own host. SANDBOX_PROVIDER=desktop is a separate, development-only configuration for backends running directly on the intended host.

Native file reads and workspace exports are limited to 8 MiB per file. A larger workspace file fails the checkpoint and preserves the previous saved workspace; local files remain on the computer. Writes are bounded by the 12 MiB encoded request limit.

  • Published images (docker-compose.images.yml) default to SANDBOX_PROVIDER=docker with a local supervisor and published ghcr.io/elie222/rakazo/computer image. No E2B account required. Optional: set e2b, novita, daytona, createos, or boat plus the matching API key for remote computers.
  • Docker is the quick-start default for published images and for a source checkout / full local Compose stack. Workspace bots share a persistent Team Computer by default; Private computers are optional. Keep the supervisor private, as the included Compose files do.
  • E2B runs bot computers away from the WhatEverFi host and is a good choice for public or multi-user production deployments. WhatEverFi checkpoints the portable workspace and browser-profile directory to DATA_DIR; the E2B disk is a runtime cache, not the durable source of truth.
  • Daytona provides the same remote-computer contract through Daytona sandboxes. Configure DAYTONA_API_KEY and optionally DAYTONA_API_URL / DAYTONA_TARGET / DAYTONA_SNAPSHOT.
  • CreateOS provides the same remote-computer contract through CreateOS desktop sandboxes. Configure CREATEOS_SANDBOX_API_KEY and optionally CREATEOS_SANDBOX_BASE_URL, CREATEOS_SANDBOX_SHAPE, or CREATEOS_SANDBOX_ROOTFS. WhatEverFi defaults to https://api.sb.createos.sh, s-2vcpu-2gb, and desktop:1.
  • Boat provides a managed Linux desktop through BOAT_API_KEY and optionally BOAT_API_URL. WhatEverFi always creates or resumes sandboxes with noEnv: true, keeps the portable workspace under /home/user/rakazo-home, and refreshes a two-hour TTL. Boat uses the shared Linux desktop runtime and protected port routes for concurrent bot desktops. Each bot has its own persistent Chrome profile; logins are not shared between bots.
  • Local computer access in the app-managed Electron instance runs commands on Windows, macOS, or Linux through the native bridge. Bots can read/change local files and launch installed apps through OS commands, subject to your account and OS permissions. Portable file tools and checkpoints remain scoped to bot workspaces; use commands for other local folders. On macOS and Windows, the owner’s own chats also get the paired-computer screen tools through the same bridge, with the same per-app approval; routines and other people’s messages do not. Permission is remembered locally and can be revoked from the app menu. Only enable this for a trusted personal instance: every bot on that instance can use your account’s permissions.
  • Desktop provider (SANDBOX_PROVIDER=desktop) runs commands directly on the API/worker host, with only a minimal shell environment (no server secrets). The API and worker refuse it unless NODE_ENV is development or test, so a production server never runs bot commands on itself. Setting this inside a container does not grant access to the physical computer. Docker deployments use the authenticated native bridge when local computer access is selected; they never silently fall back to executing on the backend host.
  • Fake is only an emulator for verification.
  • None boots the product without a computer host (fallback when Docker/supervisor is not configured, or when a remote provider is selected without its API key).

docker (in-stack supervisor)

Compose starts a sandbox supervisor (from the app image) on the internal network (port 7091 in published-images). It creates sibling computer containers from RAKAZO_COMPUTER_IMAGE + RAKAZO_COMPUTER_IMAGE_TAG.

Requirements:

  • Non-empty SANDBOX_SUPERVISOR_TOKEN (distinct from auth / screen / encryption secrets)
  • Reachable computer image (GHCR default or your mirror; on arm64 pin multi-arch tags for both app and computer)
  • Docker Engine available to the supervisor (socket mount on the Compose path)

Verify:

curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:3100/internal/health
# expect sandbox: docker

Missing supervisor token is a setup failure: do not treat sandbox: "none" as success for this path.

Signup and local Docker computers work without an E2B (or other remote) account.

Resource ceilings, network isolation and shared folders for these computers are covered in Docker computers.

Bot browser

The published computer image uses Chromium. To use Google Chrome or Brave instead, build the image with BROWSER=chrome or BROWSER=brave and point Compose at it:

docker build --build-arg BROWSER=chrome -t rakazo-computer-chrome infra/sandboxes/computer
RAKAZO_COMPUTER_IMAGE=rakazo-computer-chrome
RAKAZO_COMPUTER_IMAGE_TAG=latest

The image holds one browser, and rakazo-browser launches whichever is installed. A locally built image is not on a registry, so start the stack with bash install-images.sh --pull-never after pulling the other images once. Brave’s Rewards, Wallet, Leo, VPN and News are disabled by managed policy.

BROWSER=chrome installs Google Chrome stable from Google’s apt repository and checks Google’s signing key by fingerprint. Google publishes Chrome for amd64 only, so the build fails on other platforms; build those with the default. Chrome identifies itself as Google Chrome and ships the Widevine module that some sites expect, where Debian’s Chromium reports a plain Chromium brand and has no Widevine. Some payment and sign-in risk checks may count that profile against the device.

Browser identity is only one input to bot-check challenges; the host’s IP reputation usually matters more.

kubernetes

Each computer is one pod in a namespace you choose, created from the published computer image. The API and worker talk to the Kubernetes API with their own service account (or the kubeconfig in KUBECONFIG), so they normally run in the same cluster. No supervisor or Docker socket is involved.

Variable Default Notes
KUBERNETES_SANDBOX_NAMESPACE rakazo-sandboxes Namespace for computer pods; it must exist
KUBERNETES_SANDBOX_COMPUTER_IMAGE ghcr.io/elie222/rakazo/computer:edge Pin a digest in production
KUBERNETES_SANDBOX_RUNTIME_CLASS_NAME unset For example kata or gvisor for a VM or user-space kernel boundary
KUBERNETES_SANDBOX_CPU_LIMIT / _MEMORY_LIMIT unset Container limits, such as 2 and 4Gi
KUBERNETES_SANDBOX_POD_LABELS / _POD_ANNOTATIONS unset JSON objects of strings, merged into every pod
KUBERNETES_SANDBOX_READY_TIMEOUT_MS 120000 How long a new pod has to become ready

Each pod runs the image’s own user (uid 1000) with no service account token and no service links, with all Linux capabilities dropped, privilege escalation off and the runtime’s default seccomp profile, like a Docker computer (these apply to newly created pods; a pod that was already running keeps its old spec until it is stopped and recreated), and is labelled app.kubernetes.io/name=rakazo-computer and rakazo-bot-id=<bot id>. Commands, file transfers and workspace save and restore go through pods/exec; save and restore stream the home as one tar archive. Screens use the image’s desktop gateway on the pod IP, so the API, the worker and the web screen proxy must be able to reach pods in that namespace on port 6080 and the display ports from 6100 upward. Pods are ephemeral: the saved workspace is the persistence boundary, as with the remote providers. Kubernetes computers do not bill while running, so COMPUTER_MAX_ACTIVE_MS does not apply to them; COMPUTER_MAX_ACTIVE_UNBILLED_MS caps them when set.

Mounted home (optional)

A bot can finish its reply while its computer is still saving a large workspace. Without a mounted home, saving copies files back to the server and may pause browsers. More CPU can make that copy faster, but it does not remove the copy or its exclusive save period.

If the computer writes directly to the server’s workspace directory, those files are already saved. This is a mounted home: only DATA_DIR/homes/<home key> is mounted at /home/rakazo. Run checkpoints record a revision without exporting files or changing the computer to suspending, so they do not interrupt its screen. An intentional stop or idle shutdown still closes the screen.

This option applies to the local home store. With OBJECT_STORAGE_BUCKET configured, WhatEverFi ignores the home claim and continues copying workspaces. A mounted home retains the latest files; it is not an immutable snapshot or a backup. Keep encrypted, off-host backups of the data volume.

Start with one shared claim

The simplest layout puts the API, worker and computer pods in the same namespace. The API and worker mount the data claim at DATA_DIR; computers mount only their own subdirectory from that same claim. A new empty claim with the same name is not the same storage.

For example, if the application namespace is rakazo, its data claim is data, and API pods have label app=rakazo-api, configure both API and worker with:

SANDBOX_PROVIDER=kubernetes
KUBERNETES_SANDBOX_NAMESPACE=rakazo
KUBERNETES_SANDBOX_HOME_CLAIM=data
KUBERNETES_SANDBOX_HOME_COLOCATE_NAMESPACE=rakazo
KUBERNETES_SANDBOX_HOME_COLOCATE_LABELS={"app":"rakazo-api"}

Use your deployment’s actual namespace, claim and API label. Move the computer Role and RoleBinding below to that namespace too; keep permissions scoped to the computer manager. If application and computer pods share a namespace, distinguish them by pod labels in network and admission policies. The computer pods carry app.kubernetes.io/name=rakazo-computer.

The two HOME_COLOCATE settings are required. They keep computers on a node with the selected application pods. A ReadWriteOnce volume can be used by multiple pods on the same node; it does not mean one pod only. A ReadWriteOncePod claim is unsuitable for this shared layout. See Kubernetes volume access modes. The directory must be writable by the computer image’s uid/gid 1000. WhatEverFi sets fsGroup: 1000 and mounts the exact homes/<home key> subpath, not the whole data directory.

Keeping a separate computer namespace on k3s

A pod cannot mount another namespace’s claim. If computers must remain in rakazo-sandboxes, that namespace needs a claim exposing the same underlying directory, not a separately provisioned disk. This requires storage-specific administration.

For a single-node k3s installation using a local directory, an administrator can create a static local PV and bind it to a claim in the computer namespace. Its local.path must be the existing application data directory, and its node affinity must identify the node that owns that directory. Keep the API/worker’s existing volume and data intact. Use Retain on both PV references before making the second reference, so removing a claim cannot trigger deletion of the shared directory. Configure HOME_CLAIM with the computer-namespace claim, while HOME_COLOCATE_NAMESPACE and HOME_COLOCATE_LABELS continue to identify the application pods.

This is two references to one directory, not two copies, extra capacity, or failover. Kubernetes does not coordinate their deletion as a pair. Record that relationship in your operations notes and never clean up the directory through either reference while the other still uses it. Do not apply this technique to a CSI volume by duplicating its volume handle; use the storage provider’s supported sharing arrangement instead. See local volume requirements.

Preserve the sandbox boundary when allowing the new volume. Admission should allow only the named home PVC, mounted at /home/rakazo, with a subPath exactly equal to homes/ plus the pod’s validated rakazo-bot-id label. Reject parent paths, a mount of the entire claim, other home keys, host paths, injected credentials, and privileged containers. Keep the service-account token disabled. These restrictions constrain the pods created by the trusted computer manager; they do not make that manager an untrusted tenant. Validate admission using server-side dry runs before replacing live pods.

Move existing computers without losing their files

  1. Wait for bot jobs and manual computer sessions to finish. Stop each computer through WhatEverFi and confirm its save succeeds. Do not delete an unmounted pod first: its newest files may exist only inside that pod.
  2. Back up the data volume, including homes and home-revisions, and record checksums of representative large files. Ensure the intended claim exposes that saved directory.
  3. Apply the mounted-home settings to both API and worker, along with the storage, placement, access and admission policies for your namespace layout. Existing unmounted pods keep the old copy behavior until they are stopped and recreated.
  4. Start one computer. Inspect its pod’s volumes and mounts: the correct claim must appear at /home/rakazo with that computer’s homes/<home key> subpath. A successful boot alone does not prove the home is mounted.
  5. Compare the saved file checksums. Write a small test file in the computer, stop and start it through WhatEverFi, then verify that file again. Confirm that finishing a bot task no longer disconnects the screen during its workspace checkpoint before moving the remaining computers.

For rollback, stop computers cleanly before removing mounts or changing the storage mapping. Retain the shared directory and the backup. Removing the environment variable alone does not unmount an existing pod; WhatEverFi still detects its mounted home to avoid copying over live files. A replacement unmounted pod restores from the saved server directory.

When a computer still feels slow

Start with the operation that is waiting, rather than increasing every limit. A reasonable starting point for a browser computer is 2 CPU and 4Gi memory, adjusted to its workload. Budget for all concurrent computers plus the API, worker, database and the node’s other workloads. Keep spare disk capacity for browser profiles, uploads and backups.

What you observe What to check next
Computer is busy as a task finishes Inspect the real pod mount; an old unmounted pod still exports its home. Also check for an active boot, recovery or another computer operation.
Container restarts or OOMKilled Check pod events and memory usage. Increase the affected container’s memory only after confirming memory pressure.
CPU stays at its limit Compare usage and CPU throttling with the configured limit; increasing that limit may help.
A new pod stays Pending Describe the pod: inspect quota, available resources, claim binding and affinity. A local disk cannot follow the pod to another node.
Screen reconnects but the computer stays running Check the screen-proxy/WebSocket path and authorization separately from disk persistence.

Use kubectl top pods -n <namespace> for current CPU/memory and kubectl describe pod -n <namespace> <computer-pod> for scheduling and restart evidence. Repeat a small task and a large-file task separately, measuring startup, file operations and checkpoint time. A quick first reply does not mean the file operation or save has completed.

The API and worker service account needs this in the computer namespace:

apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: rakazo-computers
  namespace: rakazo-sandboxes
rules:
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["pods"]
    verbs: ["create", "get", "delete"]
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["pods/exec"]
    verbs: ["create", "get"]

Bind it to the service account the API and worker run as with a RoleBinding. A NetworkPolicy that admits only the API, worker and web pods to the computer pods, and denies their egress to private ranges, is recommended.

incus

Each computer is an Incus application container started from the published computer image through Incus’s OCI support (Incus 6.11 or newer; the start command’s uid needs the oci.uid and oci.gid keys). The API and worker call the Incus REST API with a client certificate; no supervisor or Docker socket is involved.

Variable Default Notes
INCUS_SANDBOX_URL none The Incus API, such as https://incus.example.test:8443
INCUS_SANDBOX_CLIENT_CERT / _CLIENT_KEY none PEM client certificate and key; \n escapes are accepted. API and worker only
INCUS_SANDBOX_SERVER_CERT unset The server’s own certificate (incus info shows it), trusted exactly. Unset uses the system CAs and the URL’s host name
INCUS_SANDBOX_PROJECT default Use a project of its own, below
INCUS_SANDBOX_COMPUTER_IMAGE ghcr.io/elie222/rakazo/computer:edge Pin a release tag or digest in production
INCUS_SANDBOX_CPU_LIMIT / _MEMORY_LIMIT / _PROCESS_LIMIT 2 / 2GiB / 2048 Incus limits.cpu, limits.memory and limits.processes of each computer

Computers without the URL, certificate or key fall back to none.

Each instance is unprivileged, without nesting, with an isolated id map (its own range of host uids) and the limits above, all set on the instance so a profile cannot loosen them. The image’s own start command and every command run as uid 1000, set on the instance and on each exec rather than taken from the image’s user, with no privilege escalation, the same boundary as a Docker computer, so a custom image must keep that command.

Each start creates a new instance named rakazo-<uuid> and labelled user.rakazo-bot-id=<bot id>; one carrying another bot’s id is never reused or deleted. Instances are ephemeral: Incus deletes one when it stops, and the saved workspace is the persistence boundary, copied in when a computer starts and saved back when it stops, as on Kubernetes. Only cache paths and the screen size are set in the instance environment. Incus computers do not bill while running, so COMPUTER_MAX_ACTIVE_UNBILLED_MS caps them when set. The first computer downloads the image into the project, which can take a few minutes.

The instance’s root disk and network come from the project’s default profile. Screens use the image’s desktop gateway on the instance address, so the API, the worker and the web screen proxy must reach that network on port 6100, for example by running them on the Incus host or in an instance on a network the host routes to the computers.

Restricted project and certificate

Give WhatEverFi a project and a client certificate that can reach nothing else. A restricted certificate cannot change its project’s restrictions or limits. On the Incus host:

incus network create rakazo0
incus network acl create rakazo-computers
# Public internet only: no host, LAN, link-local, multicast or cloud-metadata addresses.
incus network acl rule add rakazo-computers egress action=reject \
  destination=0.0.0.0/8,10.0.0.0/8,100.64.0.0/10,127.0.0.0/8,169.254.0.0/16,172.16.0.0/12,192.0.0.0/24,192.168.0.0/16,198.18.0.0/15,224.0.0.0/3
incus network acl rule add rakazo-computers egress action=reject protocol=tcp \
  destination=::1/128,fc00::/7,fe80::/10,ff00::/8
incus network acl rule add rakazo-computers egress action=reject protocol=udp \
  destination=::1/128,fc00::/7,fe80::/10,ff00::/8
incus network acl rule add rakazo-computers egress action=reject protocol=icmp6 icmp_type=128 \
  destination=::1/128,fc00::/7,fe80::/10
# Screens, from the address the API, worker and web connect from.
incus network acl rule add rakazo-computers ingress action=allow protocol=tcp \
  source=<rakazo-server-address> destination_port=6100

incus project create rakazo -c features.images=true -c features.profiles=true \
  -c restricted=true -c restricted.networks.access=rakazo0 \
  -c restricted.images.servers=ghcr.io
incus profile device add default root disk path=/ pool=default --project rakazo
incus profile device add default eth0 nic network=rakazo0 --project rakazo \
  security.acls=rakazo-computers security.acls.default.egress.action=allow \
  security.ipv4_filtering=true security.ipv6_filtering=true

openssl req -x509 -newkey ec -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:secp384r1 -nodes -days 3650 \
  -subj /CN=rakazo -keyout rakazo.key -out rakazo.crt
incus config trust add-certificate rakazo.crt --restricted --projects rakazo

The ACL sits on each computer’s network device, so it also keeps computers from reaching each other and other instances on the bridge; it needs the nftables firewall driver. Connections to a computer are refused except to the screen port. IPv6 neighbour discovery keeps working because only echo requests are refused among ICMPv6 messages to private addresses; DHCP and DNS from the bridge are allowed by Incus before any ACL rule. The IP filtering options stop a computer from spoofing addresses or sending router advertisements to the host. Set INCUS_SANDBOX_PROJECT=rakazo and the certificate and key from rakazo.crt and rakazo.key.

wuying

Bot computers run on one existing Wuying (无影) cloud computer. An admin can also set this up in Settings → Computer instead of these variables; see Wuying cloud computers for the full setup. Each computer’s home is a folder under the desktop user’s profile (%USERPROFILE%\rakazo\<home>), and the desktop’s own disk keeps it between stops, so nothing is copied in or out. Commands run in PowerShell; files, screenshots and input go through the desktop’s MCP gateway. Stopping the last computer on it powers the desktop off; deleting one removes only its home folder, never the desktop.

Variable Notes
WUYING_ACCESS_KEY_ID / WUYING_ACCESS_KEY_SECRET RAM user allowed ecd:DescribeDesktops, ecd:StartDesktops, ecd:StopDesktops and appstream-center:GetAuthCode. API and worker only
WUYING_REGION_ID Defaults to cn-hangzhou
WUYING_DESKTOP_ID The cloud computer, assigned to the end user below
WUYING_END_USER_ID Screen logins are issued for this user
WUYING_MCP_URL / WUYING_MCP_TOKEN The desktop’s MCP gateway and its bearer token

The web and Electron screen is drawn by the Wuying Web SDK in /computer-screen/screen.html, served by the web app. Mobile rejects the custom screen URL and does not embed this SDK. The SDK is not committed; fetch the pinned release before building the web app:

node scripts/wuying-web-sdk.mjs

The SDK runs in an opaque-origin sandboxed frame with an in-memory storage shim and a no-op cookie accessor in both its launcher and nested runtime. A CSP scoped to /computer-screen/ permits the vendor hosts, blob workers and WebAssembly compilation. The one-time login code stays only in the URL fragment, outside HTTP requests and Referer.

All bots, users and spaces configured with this provider, including Private Computers, share the same Windows desktop and account permissions, including files outside their workspace folders. Use it only in a trusted deployment. The gateway bounds each call to one minute, 16 KiB of command output and 1,000 folder entries. A command allowed longer than a minute runs detached with its output in files under %USERPROFILE%\rakazo\.runs, read back every second and removed when it ends or is cancelled.

none

Runs API/web without provisioning bot computers.

Remote providers

Set SANDBOX_PROVIDER to exactly one of:

Value Credential Notes
e2b E2B_API_KEY Hosted sandboxes
novita NOVITA_API_KEY Build the desktop template first; optional SANDBOX_TEMPLATE
daytona DAYTONA_API_KEY Optional DAYTONA_API_URL, DAYTONA_TARGET, DAYTONA_SNAPSHOT
boat BOAT_API_KEY Optional BOAT_API_URL (see .env.example)
boxd BOXD_API_KEY Optional BOXD_ORG to create computers in a boxd organization
instabox INSTABOX_API_KEY Computers start in the key’s organization; see instabox computers
createos CREATEOS_SANDBOX_API_KEY Optional CREATEOS_SANDBOX_BASE_URL, CREATEOS_SANDBOX_SHAPE, CREATEOS_SANDBOX_ROOTFS
railway RAILWAY_API_TOKEN and RAILWAY_ENVIRONMENT_ID Optional RAILWAY_SANDBOX_REGION; RAILWAY_MAX_WORKSPACE_FILE_BYTES (default 64 MiB) caps each workspace file WhatEverFi reads or saves. Railway supplies the environment ID when WhatEverFi runs there; see the Railway template
wuying WUYING_* (below) One existing Wuying cloud computer (Windows)

Remote paths still need a working API/worker; they do not replace Postgres or the web UI. They require egress to the provider. For air-gapped hosts prefer docker with pre-loaded images, or none.

A run starts its computer only when it first uses a computer tool. With idle sleep on, a computer suspends after SANDBOX_IDLE_MS idle. On providers that bill while running (E2B, Daytona, Boat, boxd, instabox, CreateOS, Railway), it also suspends after COMPUTER_MAX_ACTIVE_MS (default 2 hours) up in one stretch, even with background work or an open screen, unless a run is executing on it, a user is in control of its screen, or a coding agent CLI (Codex, Claude Code, OpenCode) wrote its session within the last SANDBOX_IDLE_MS. An agent waiting at its prompt writes nothing, so it does not hold the computer. 0 turns the cap off. That exception lifts only the uptime cap; idle suspension after SANDBOX_IDLE_MS still applies once nothing holds the computer. Docker, Kubernetes and Incus computers are capped only when COMPUTER_MAX_ACTIVE_UNBILLED_MS is set (off by default; minimum 60000), with the same exceptions, so an abandoned background command cannot keep one running for days. Like every cap, it needs idle sleep on: SANDBOX_IDLE_MS=0 turns it off too. This-Mac computers are never capped. The next use resumes it. Asking for takeover restarts the idle timer, and on providers that do not bill while running the run also holds the computer for 30 minutes after asking, so the user can answer the push on the same open page.

Computer run time

Each stretch a computer runs at its provider is a row in computer_runs, attributed to the computer’s owner and space. A run starts when the computer becomes ready (boot time is not counted) and ends when it stops. endReason says how: stopped, idle, active_limit, replaced (update, recovery, or reset), gone (the provider had already stopped or lost the sandbox), deleted, or reconciled (the end was never seen; the worker found the computer no longer running). For gone and reconciled, endedAt is when WhatEverFi noticed, so the true end may be earlier. The worker also opens the run of a running computer whose start was not recorded. An open run whose computer still reads as running is a computer that may be left on. Deleting a user or space keeps their runs with userId and spaceId cleared. This-Mac computers are not recorded.

The table has row-level security, so query it as the database owner. Timestamps are UTC. Run hours per user over the last 7 days, counting runs still open up to now:

WITH now_utc AS (SELECT now() AT TIME ZONE 'UTC' AS at)
SELECT r."userId", u.email,
       round(sum(extract(epoch FROM
         coalesce(r."endedAt", n.at) - greatest(r."startedAt", n.at - interval '7 days')
       )) / 3600, 1) AS hours
FROM computer_runs r
CROSS JOIN now_utc n
LEFT JOIN "user" u ON u.id = r."userId"
WHERE coalesce(r."endedAt", n.at) > n.at - interval '7 days'
GROUP BY r."userId", u.email
ORDER BY hours DESC;

Runs open longer than 6 hours:

SELECT r."computerId", r."userId", r."spaceId", r.kind, r."startedAt",
       round(extract(epoch FROM (now() AT TIME ZONE 'UTC') - r."startedAt") / 3600, 1) AS hours_open
FROM computer_runs r
WHERE r."endedAt" IS NULL
  AND r."startedAt" < (now() AT TIME ZONE 'UTC') - interval '6 hours'
ORDER BY r."startedAt";

Linux background-work inspection

The fallback background-work probe and cancellation commands require Bash, Python 3.7 or newer, and a readable/searchable /proc root. Both supplied images install python3 explicitly in infra/sandboxes/computer/Dockerfile and infra/sandboxes/desktop/Dockerfile. Custom and remote images must provide this capability. The scanner itself never installs Python.

The scanner reads marker file descriptors regardless of the holder’s UID, including duplicated, inherited, and deleted-but-open markers. Individual entries that disappear or deny access are skipped because their links cannot be observed. A failed root traversal, unexpected filesystem error, or missing Python capability makes inspection unknown. Such failures do not authorize marker cleanup or cancellation signals from partial scanner output. Cancellation rechecks each selected PID’s marker descriptors before signaling it.

E2B computer template

E2B computers start from the rakazo-computer template: E2B’s stock desktop at 2 vCPU and 4 GB instead of its 8 vCPU and 8 GB. Build it once in the E2B team that owns E2B_API_KEY, and again whenever its definition in packages/adapters/src/e2b-template.ts changes:

E2B_API_KEY=<deployment key> pnpm sandbox:e2b-template

Until it exists, new computers use the stock desktop template. Existing computers keep the size they were created with until they are replaced.

Novita computer template

Set SANDBOX_PROVIDER=novita and NOVITA_API_KEY on both the API and worker. Build the desktop template once in the account that owns that key:

NOVITA_API_KEY=<deployment-key> pnpm sandbox:novita-template

The rakazo-computer template uses Novita’s desktop image at 2 vCPU and 4 GB. The provider requires this template and does not fall back to the larger stock desktop. To use another desktop template, set SANDBOX_TEMPLATE to the same name when building and on both services. Rebuild when the template definition changes; existing computers keep their original template and resources.

Computers pause on idle timeout and on stop, preserving files, browser profiles, and running-process memory. Reconnecting resumes the same computer. Destruction deletes it without resuming it. Stop retries pause requests and checks the remote state. Command cancellation and deadlines retry termination; if termination cannot be confirmed, the adapter attempts to pause the computer and reports that the command may remain suspended. An unconfirmed command stop also quarantines the computer in the shared database, so API heartbeats, worker jobs, and restarts cannot silently resume it. Use the existing Recover or Reset action to replace it from saved work; the paused guest is preserved until that explicit action. Normal reads and heartbeats do not resume a paused Novita computer. An outage can prevent both operations; the configured idle timeout remains the final auto-pause boundary. This recovery does not delete the saved computer. Paused storage remains subject to Novita’s storage billing and retention terms. This provider uses the shared Linux desktop runtime for screens, takeover, terminal, and portable workspace transfer.

A missing key disables computers without preventing startup. A present but invalid key, a missing template, or a quota failure surfaces when a computer starts; an authentication or network error does not authorize replacing an existing computer.

Boat computer snapshot

Boat computers start from a named snapshot, rakazo-computer-<hash>, that already has the desktop tools installed. The hash follows the setup in packages/adapters/src/boat-sandbox.ts, so changing it produces a new name and existing computers keep the one they started from.

No setup is needed: when the snapshot for the current setup is missing, the API or worker logs sandbox.base_image with outcome: "missing", builds it once in the background from a fresh sandbox with no account environment and no bot data, and deletes the build sandbox. Until it is ready, new computers install the tools themselves. To build it ahead of the first computer, in the Boat account that owns BOAT_API_KEY:

BOAT_API_KEY=<deployment key> pnpm sandbox:boat-snapshot

boxd computers

boxd computers are isolated microVMs: no boxd credentials inside, and no route to the account’s other machines. They start from a snapshot, rakazo-computer-<hash>, with the desktop tools and Chrome installed, built the same way as Boat’s: once in the background when missing, from a fresh machine that is deleted afterwards. To build it ahead of the first computer:

BOXD_API_KEY=<deployment key> pnpm sandbox:boxd-snapshot

The desktop is served on the machine’s own public HTTPS address; every screen and terminal still needs its own token, which the desktop gateway checks. Stopping a computer suspends it with its memory, so programs it was running continue when it resumes.

instabox computers

instabox computers start from instabox’s own desktop image, which already has Chromium; the first start installs the rest of the desktop tools in a few seconds. They are created without the instabox account’s vault, so secrets saved on that account never reach a bot’s computer.

The desktop is served on the computer’s public HTTPS address; every screen and terminal still needs its own token, which the desktop gateway checks. Stopping a computer suspends it with its memory. instabox also pauses a computer after 30 idle minutes, later than the default SANDBOX_IDLE_MS, so WhatEverFi normally stops it first. One key’s computers share its account’s limits on requests at once (API calls, and connections to screens and terminals), so a deployment with many active computers at the same time can see them slow down.

Verify a provider change

After changing provider or keys (from the published-images drop directory that holds docker-compose.images.yml and .env):

docker compose --env-file .env -f docker-compose.images.yml up -d
curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:3100/internal/health

Confirm sandbox equals the intended provider (e2b, novita, daytona, boat, boxd, or instabox). HTTP 200 alone does not verify a remote provider: a missing API key falls back to sandbox: "none". A present but invalid key still reports the selected provider. Open a bot’s computer to verify provisioning and desktop access.
